title: Your reading plan
hook: choose one text to keep reading after the summit
tomorrow: seventy days a guest. what does a good guest say at the door?

segments.voice: Yesterday, separate shelves: each book honored the way its own people read it. Today the shelves get very real, because only one book fits in the bag.

A child's voice drifts over a garden wall, chanting the same words again and again. On the other side, under a fig tree, a teacher of speech, learned and restless, sits weeping, unable to change his life. The voice says: "Take up and read; Take up and read." In his Latin, tolle lege. You can't keep every book; this man was about to find the one he'd keep.
screen: `A CHILD'S VOICE OVER A WALL.` → `A MAN UNDER A FIG TREE.` → `TAKE UP AND READ.`

segments.voice: The man is Augustine; this reading opened in his garden, and now it closes there. He tells the story in his Confessions. He can't remember any children's game with those words, so he takes them as a command. He goes back to the bench where he left a book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads the first passage his eyes fall on: not in rioting and drunkenness, not in strife and envying, but "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He writes that he didn't want to read further, and had no need to. A light seemed to pour into his heart, and the doubt was gone. Notice the senses in it. A child's voice over a wall. The weight of a book in the hand. One passage, not a library. Here's the teaching. Some Christian teachers point to Augustine's garden as a picture of a way of reading: scripture taken up not as information, but as a word addressed to the reader, a passage at a time, read slowly enough to change a life. A detail worth keeping: the voice that turned Augustine around came from a child next door, and he never says whose it was. That's the companion-text idea. One book, kept close, opened often. Choosing it isn't turning away from the rest of the shelf.
screen: `AUGUSTINE UNDER THE FIG TREE.` · `ONE PASSAGE, AND NO NEED TO READ ON.` · `A VOICE, A WEIGHT, A PAGE.` · `ONE BOOK, KEPT CLOSE.` · then, large: `MY COMPANION TEXT.`

segments.voice: Pick up a book you might keep reading, any book that matters to you, or open one text on your phone. Feel its weight, open it anywhere, and read one line out loud, slowly, twice. Then close it and rest your hand on the cover for the rest of the time.
Your reading plan: one companion text, taken up and read, a little at a time.
Hold onto this: my companion text, one book kept close and opened often. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Augustine's 'take up and read' (Confessions 8.12) is retold in Christian teaching about reading scripture slowly and personally; some readers, on any path, keep one text close and read a little of it each day.
